articles.title: US bank stocks' longest losing streak since 2008 clashes with earnings picture
articles.summary: The benchmark KBW Nasdaq Bank Index fell slightly on Monday and has sold off for the past six consecutive weeks.
articles.body:
US bank stocks are suffering their longest losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis, despite some of the country's biggest lenders having so far reported another sturdy set of earnings.

Results from the four biggest lenders last week gave fresh evidence that their US consumer and business customers are holding up even in the face of sharply elevated borrowing costs.

JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Bank of America ( BAC ), Citigroup ( C ), and Wells Fargo ( WFC ) collectively set aside $7.6 billion in credit provisions during the quarter, down about 3% from a year earlier. Actual loan losses in the quarter between these same banks fell 5%, while lending grew nearly 10%.

Investors still appear unconvinced. The benchmark KBW Nasdaq Bank Index ( ^BKX ) fell slightly on Monday. It has sold off for the past six consecutive weeks, losing 11% since early September in its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis, according to Yahoo Finance data.

The sell-off comes as credit managers worldwide appear increasingly worried about what happens next.

A recent survey of credit portfolio managers at major banks and other global financial institutions found that about 60% expect corporate defaults to rise worldwide over the next 12 months, while 85% anticipate wider spreads on North American junk bonds over the next three months. The figure is sharply higher compared to the survey's second quarter reading of a 40% rise in corporate defaults over the next 12 months and 50% increase in North American junk bonds in the ensuing three months.

Credit portfolio managers "are seeing some risk appetite among investors, but they are also seeing a number of companies, which have so far managed to stay afloat, beginning to reach the end of the line," Som-lok Leung, executive director for the International Association of Credit Portfolio Managers, said in an emailed statement.

Morgan Stanley analysts said in a Monday note to clients that bank credit conditions remain largely "benign," apart from isolated commercial weakness, although executives have sounded generally more cautious on earnings calls so far this month than in the second quarter.

Investor worries center on whether persistently higher interest rates will eventually squeeze borrowers. By the same logic, declining interest rates have "the potential to engineer a bounce" in bank stocks, Bank of America analyst Ebrahim Poonawala wrote Monday.

"Ideally, that occurs on the back of lower energy prices or easing inflation," Poonawala added.

articles.title: Rural America can’t grow if its workers can’t find a place to live
articles.summary: Rep. Max Miller argues that housing shortages in rural Ohio hinder economic development and calls for federal support to ensure workers can afford to live in their communities.
articles.body:
A hospital in Holmes County, Ohio, recruits a physician. The offer is accepted. Then the doctor spends weeks looking for a house, finds nothing, and takes a job somewhere else.

That story came out of community listening sessions in Wayne and Holmes counties this summer, where employers said housing shortages have made hiring increasingly difficult and that some workers, physicians included, left the area because they could not find a place to live.

The workforce is here. The jobs are here. The homes are missing. What employers are seeing in rural Ohio is a warning for communities across the country: a housing shortage can become an economic development problem.

The numbers confirm what employers already know. A countywide housing study presented to Millersburg Village Council in August identified demand for roughly 858 additional owner-occupied homes and 280 rental units in Holmes County, and found that only 44 percent of the county’s workers actually live there, compared with about 54 percent in surrounding rural counties. Many workers commute from elsewhere, while local employers struggle to recruit and retain people who want to live nearby.

Wayne County has 26 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income households. Statewide, Ohio faces a shortage of roughly 266,000 rental homes affordable and available to those households, according to the 2026 Gap Report from the National Low Income Housing Coalition and the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio. Ohio is a microcosm of a national shortage: across the country, there are only 35 such homes for every 100 extremely low-income households, a shortfall of 7.2 million homes . The Ohio Housing Finance Agency’s 2026 assessment documents a net loss of more than 62,000 rental units affordable to very low-income Ohioans since 2019. A full-time Ohio worker now needs to earn $23.82 an hour to afford a two-bedroom apartment. The average renter earns $19.59.

Those figures describe nurses, line workers, teachers, and young families in Medina, Wooster and Millersburg. They also reflect pressures felt in communities well beyond Ohio. These are the people who keep small towns running.

The barriers are familiar to anyone who has tried to build in rural Ohio or in small towns across America: high land prices, infrastructure costs that fall hard on small municipalities, and development rules written for a different era. Every one of those obstacles adds cost, and every added dollar prices out another working family.

Congress needs more people to care about housing. As it becomes a luxury to have a mortgage, we are seeing fewer Americans have families, put down roots, and live the American Dream we all try to achieve. Veterans face housing challenges, too, especially when a new job or assignment requires a move. That’s why I introduced the Homes for Heroes Act , which would increase the maximum VA loan guarantee available to eligible veterans with an outstanding VA-backed mortgage from 25 to 37.5 percent of the conforming loan limit, making it easier for them to purchase another home when they need to relocate.

This summer, Congress delivered the most significant federal housing legislation in a generation. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act passed the House 358-32 and the Senate 85-5 before becoming law on July 11. The law cuts regulatory delays, modernizes manufactured housing rules, allows pre-approved home designs so builders can get permits faster, and allows rental assistance to continue when USDA mortgages mature. The Agriculture Department’s rural multifamily portfolio includes roughly 400,000 affordable rental units nationwide.

That vote was the easy part. The hard part is implementation, and I intend to make sure rural communities, including those in Ohio, get their share. That means pressing the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Agriculture Department to move grant dollars to communities like ours instead of letting them pool in large metros. It means working with county commissioners and village councils on the zoning and infrastructure decisions that determine whether a project pencils out. And it means supporting the state programs already producing results: Ohio’s housing tax credit, created in the 2023 budget, is helping finance new affordable homes.

I stood at the groundbreaking for The Lafayette in Medina County, a supportive housing development that exists because local leaders, developers, and government worked together. That model works. It needs to happen a hundred more times across this district and in small communities nationwide.

Rural Ohio has always been willing to work. The same is true of rural America. Our job in Washington is to make sure there is somewhere for those workers to live.

Max Miller represents Ohio’s 7th District in Congress.

articles.title: Last week saw the largest tech sell skew in more than 5 years, Jefferies says
articles.summary: Last week was bloody for tech stocks, Jefferies says.
articles.body:
Jefferies' equity trading desk saw its most heavily selling-tilted tech trading week in more than five years, analysts said over the weekend, putting a finer point on the CoreWeave-led tech sell-off that dominated markets last week.

"Simply put, there's a tremendous amount of angst in the market right now, and from our conversations and flows, there's been a very consistent and violent de-gross occurring over the last several sessions," Jeffrey Favuzza, TMT equity strategist at Jefferies, wrote to clients.

By market close on Friday, the week's skew in tech equities had reached $7.5 billion in net selling activity — a significant jump over the $5.5 billion skew ahead of the opening bell on Friday and a testament to heavy selling into the weekend.

The jump in outflow activity was enough to push the week's skew past that of the "DeepSeek moment" week in January 2025, when the Chinese AI lab released its open-weight DeepSeek model and set off a flurry of concerns that US labs would see their revenues fall as enterprises turned to cheaper foreign options, the analysts said.

Selling activity through Jefferies' equity trading desk was most concentrated last week in semiconductors, memory, hardware, and communications equipment subsectors, Favuzza noted, while only horizontal software and IT/info services subsectors saw a notable buy skew on the week.

That split matched activity in the wider market, where the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell by roughly 3% while the Philadelphia Semiconductor index ( ^SOX ) lost 10%.

Much of the problem, Favuzza noted, lies with an increasingly sketchy financing picture. Part and parcel of the AI boom is the explosion in capex across the sector, with capex by hyperscalers alone expected to exceed $800 billion in 2026 and cross $1 trillion next year.

That spending has collided with a range of factors — the war in Iran, growing US debt , trade turmoil — that have pushed the international bond complex into a deep sell-off, sending yields on government debt from the US and other nations to multi-decade highs "at the same time that the hyperscalers have flooded the market with paper this year."

Last week's sell-off was largely catalyzed by spiking credit risk and worries about the worthiness of debt issuance at CoreWeave ( CRWV ), a so-called neocloud that's heavily backed by Nvidia ( NVDA ).

"While the underlying demand for the Neos hasn't downticked," Favuzza wrote to clients, "the confidence in some of their access to cheaper capital has."

The tech trade has also lost some of the momentum-driven wind in its sails, Favuzza said, arguing that "we never recovered, both from a price and conviction standpoint, from the Momentum meltdown of the summer." Not only was last week the worst in more than five years by sell skew, but it was also the second-worst week for the tech momentum pair (buying winning tech stocks while selling losers) in more than 20 years, beaten out only by a COVID-19 sell-off.

articles.title: Netflix, Trying to Please Everyone, Misses the Buzzy Shows
articles.summary: In its bid to provide something for everyone, Netflix Inc. lost the one thing that set it apart from every other streaming service — a movie or series that c...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- In its bid to provide something for everyone, Netflix Inc. lost the one thing that set it apart from every other streaming service — a movie or series that captured the cultural zeitgeist.

Netflix has forged partnerships with YouTube stars Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober, wrote big checks to woo popular podcasters like Jay Shetty and got in the game with the NFL, Major League Baseball and the FIFA Women's World Cup, in a bid to diversity its entertainment options and entice viewers.

But it has lacked a breakthrough hit like the 2025 limited series Adolescence, which garnered critical acclaim on its way to becoming one of Netflix's most popular shows of all time. Netflix's overall share of TV viewing fell to 7.8% in July, down a from 8.8% in the same period last year, according to Nielsen data. Competitors including Amazon.com Inc.'s Prime Video, Comcast Corp.'s Peacock and Skydance Corp.'s Paramount+ gained share.

Last week, the company announced it was laying off 6% of its staff and replacing Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice, a Walt Disney Co. and 21st Century Fox veteran. On Monday, the company said film chief Dan Lin was also leaving.

Netflix delivered double-digit revenue growth in its most recent quarter. Still, a slowdown in sales and viewers, as well as a failed attempt to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.'s studios and streaming business, has been weighing on Netflix shares, which are down about 26% this year. On Tuesday, Netflix is expected to show the weakest percentage increase in revenue in three years when it reports results.

"The growth is still there, but it's slower," said Hal Vogel, a longtime media analyst and author of Entertainment Industry Economics. "It's not the same Netflix. I'm sure if they had a hit series the stock would pop up for a while."

The service has lost top talent, including filmmakers David Fincher, Noah Baumbach and Shawn Levy, as well as the Duffer brothers, creators of the hit series Stranger Things, fueling concern among the company's senior-most leaders that it is no longer viewed as a haven for Hollywood's best storytellers. At the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last month, Netflix co-Chief Executive Officer Ted Sarandos rejected the idea that those departures were indicative of a problem. "They're individual cases," he said.

articles.title: Chuck Schumer urges FCC to block AI robocalls before elections
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer urges FCC to reject petition allowing AI robocalls ahead of key November midterm elections.
articles.body:
United States Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York has urged the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) not to approve a petition by the conservative group Club for Growth to allow AI-generated robocalls ahead of the November midterm elections.

“Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and, at worst, a blatant lie,” Schumer said on Monday.

The petition was originally filed on August 31, and the public comment period began on September 4 and expires on Monday.

Earlier this month , Anna Gomez, the Democratic member of the FCC, urged her colleagues not to allow consideration of the petition brought by the national conservative fiscal policy organisation.

Her concerns echoed Schumer’s. “[If] the FCC allows a dark money group to flood Americans’ phones with AI-generated robocalls they never agreed to receive, it would bring chaos so close to Election Day,” commissioner Gomez told the Reuters news agency at the time.

There is precedent for the concerns being raised. In the 2024 presidential election, ahead of the New Hampshire primary, voters received an AI-generated version in the voice of President Joe Biden, the then Democratic incumbent, telling them not to vote. The FCC said that a political consultant working with longshot primary challenger Dean Phillips was responsible.

At the state level, Louisiana, Tennessee and Vermont passed laws this year requiring disclosures for AI-generated campaign phone calls. While robocalls have been used in political campaigns for years, FCC rules prohibit such calls to cellphones without prior consent, but the restrictions do not apply to landlines.

Club for Growth’s president, David McIntosh, in a statement earlier this month, said that the group is asking for “the FCC to treat First Amendment-protected political speech the same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts, and doctor’s appointments”.

“There is no one at the FCC that has expressed any interest in moving to an order on this or any of the petitions, and there are zero plans to do so. The FCC seeks comment on petitions that come in as a matter of normal procedure,” a spokesperson for the FCC told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Dimon says US economy ‘booming,’ but warns about ‘inflationary’ events
articles.summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said in an interview published Monday that the U.S. economy, while performing well, has to fend off “inflationary” events. “The American economy is kind of booming right now. It’s good times,” Dimon told Alan Murray of The Wall Street Journal Leadership Institute. Dimon noted that corporate profits are “way up,”…
articles.body:
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said in an interview published Monday that the U.S. economy, while performing well, has to fend off “inflationary” events .

“The American economy is kind of booming right now. It’s good times,” Dimon told Alan Murray of The Wall Street Journal Leadership Institute.

Dimon noted that corporate profits are “way up,” corporations and consumers are “not overleveraged” and the unemployment rate is “really low.”

The unemployment rate has remained below 5 percent since September 2021 and was 4.2 percent last month, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

Inflation, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI), ticked up from 3.4 percent in August to 3.7 percent in September, the BLS reported last week. Wholesale prices were also up 1.3 percent month over month in September, a surge driven by elevated energy prices amid the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

Real average hourly earnings were down 0.7 percent from September 2025 to last month, according to the BLS . During his interview with Murray, Dimon said “you can argue whether” wages are going up “enough” for lower-income Americans.

“Probably not, but they have jobs, and that is the single most important thing for most people, that they have a job and they go to work,” the JPMorgan Chase CEO added.

But Dimon still warned about a slew of economic developments that could raise prices. Those events included mounting government deficits for global powers, the “remilitarization” of the world and the “restructuring” of trade agreements and healthcare systems.

Annual inflation, based on the CPI, has increased during the Iran conflict , after it was 2.4 percent the month before the war.

Long term, Dimon argued that investment in AI capabilities will spur growth and lower government deficits. But as of right now, the AI build-out is having an inflationary effect on the economy, he noted.

Dimon also said the federal government should reform its immigration system to boost the workforce, a move he predicted would benefit the economy.

“If we allowed … merit-based, proper asylum … more people working, seasonal workers, that actually would grow the economy and reduce inflation,” Dimon remarked.

articles.title: El Gobierno mantendrá el Ingreso Mínimo Vital a quienes encuentren empleo aunque sus rentas suban más de 6.000 euros
articles.standfirst: Esto es posible gracias a la última reforma regulada por el Real Decreto 240/2026
articles.summary: Esto es posible gracias a la última reforma regulada por el Real Decreto 240/2026
articles.body: El Gobierno permite mantener el Ingreso Mínimo Vital (IMV) tras conseguir un empleo o aumentar las horas de trabajo, incluso si las rentas familiares aumentan más de 6.000 euros anuales. Esto es posible gracias a la última reforma regulada por el Real Decreto 240/2026, que simplificó el denominado incentivo al empleo. El objetivo de esta normativa es garantizar que trabajar siempre resulte rentable y evitar que los beneficiarios rechacen ofertas laborales por miedo a perder la prestación inmediatamente. ¿Cómo funciona el incentivo si tus ingresos suben más de 6.000 euros? Pues bien, el sistema aplica una serie de exenciones escalonadas sobre el incremento de tus ingresos del año anterior para calcular el nuevo importe de la ayuda. Los primeros 6.000 euros de aumento quedan al 100% exentos, es decir, no reducen la cuantía del IMV. A partir de 6.000 euros (Tramo general), se queda exento al 50%, por lo que sólo computa la mitad del dinero. Finalmente, a partir de 6.000 euros (unidades con discapacidad o monoparentales) queda exento al 55%. Solo computa el 45% del excedente, ofreciendo mayor protección. A continuación, ponemos un ejemplo práctico para que se comprenda de forma más sencilla. Si una persona que cobra el IMV empieza a trabajar y sus ingresos anuales aumentan en 10.000 euros, el cálculo de la Seguridad Social para revisar la ayuda será el siguiente: Los primeros 6.000 euros quedan totalmente perdonados (0 euros a computar). De los 4.000 euros restantes, se aplica la exención del 50% (quedan exentos 2.000 euros). De los 10.000 euros nuevos que ha ganado, el Gobierno solo contará 2.000 euros como incremento de renta a la hora de restar de su IMV garantizado.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia cancels next week’s ‘Davos in the Desert’ conference after series of Houthi attacks
articles.summary: In a major setback for the kingdom’s economic ambitions, Saudi Arabia has canceled a major conference scheduled for next week in Riyadh amid a wave of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants.
articles.body: In a major setback for the kingdom’s economic ambitions, Saudi Arabia has canceled a major conference scheduled for next week in Riyadh amid a wave of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants. Known as “Davos in the Desert,” the Future Investment Initiative will now take place on an undisclosed date in 2027, according to a statement from the conference shared via email with CNN’s Becky Anderson. Normally, the annual event showcases Saudi Arabia’s financial muscle and growing role on the world stage. Wall Street leaders including JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon and BlackRock boss Larry Fink were all scheduled to speak at next week’s event. However, the FII decided to cancel the October 26-29 conference in the wake of a series of Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital, including a deadly missile strike earlier this month on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. The decision comes after a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and other strategic sites, prompting a number of countries to issue travel warnings. Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have exchanged near-daily missile, drone and air strikes in recent week, with the conflict escalating sharply.Some boards of directors may have balked at sending their CEOs into Saudi Arabia in the midst of the deadly battle with the Houthis. “This decision has been taken to ensure that our milestone tenth edition delivers the full scale, quality and impact that our partners, members, speakers and delegates expect,” the FII Institute, which runs the conference, said in the statement.Organizers said the new dates in 2027 for the event “will be communicated very soon” and all registrations and partnerships “remain valid.”The cancellation of this year’s event is a blow to Saudi Arabia’s efforts to diversify the oil-rich country’s economy away from oil and natural gas.The deteriorating security situation undermines decades of effort to attract Western capital to the Middle East and may herald a period of investment uncertainty that would be detrimental to the whole region.

articles.title: Tesla-SpaceX merger is 'not so easy': Analyst
articles.summary: Speculation about a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla is intensifying, with Wall Street analysts outlining how a deal could take shape.
articles.body:
Wall Street chatter about a possible merger between rocket maker SpaceX ( SPCX ) and EV giant Tesla ( TSLA ) has been increasing in recent weeks, with speculation about what such a deal would look like.

"It's not so easy. Basically, SpaceX would have to acquire Tesla. We think it'd be an all-stock deal," Tom Narayan, RBC Capital Markets lead equity analyst, told Yahoo Finance.

Currently, CEO Elon Musk controls 85% of SpaceX voting rights and 20% for Tesla.

"There would have to be a pretty strong premium in order to acquire Tesla," Narayan said. "We think something like a $480 stock price for Tesla; it's our price target."

Wall Street has been speculating about the merger, given synergies between SpaceX's involvement in AI, satellites, and data centers and Tesla's robotaxis and humanoid-robot initiatives.

Narayan noted the longer-term play may focus on Terafab — Elon Musk's ambitious semiconductor initiative aimed at bringing chip manufacturing in-house and reducing production costs by up to 90%.

"This is their way of bypassing Nvidia and bypassing TSMC," Narayn said. "If they can do that, it's huge."

Tesla is coming off the jaw-dropping unveiling of its Roadster EV last week.

Shares of the EV maker are down roughly 18% year to date, trading near $367 on Monday.

SpaceX went public in a blockbuster IPO this past June, pricing shares at $135 before they opened at $150.

On Monday, SpaceX stock was trading near $148.

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: ‘Tariff Man’ finally found tariffs he doesn’t like
articles.summary: President Donald Trump loves tariffs so much that during his first term, he nicknamed himself “Tariff Man.”
articles.body: President Donald Trump loves tariffs so much that during his first term, he nicknamed himself “Tariff Man.” Trump tripled down on tariffs during his second term, lobbing them on friends and enemies alike, in an attempt to revive American manufacturing, crack down on illegal drugs and even to protest an alleged “witch hunt” against an ally in Brazil. After spiking tariffs last year to the highest level since the Great Depression, Trump posted photos of himself headlined “Mister Tariff” and “The Tariff King.” But when it came to keeping sky-high tariffs on Russia, Tariff Man balked. On Friday, Trump ignited bipartisan uproar when he signed an executive order that waived new sanctions and tariffs on Russia two days before they would go into effect. Those penalties were contained in a bill Trump signed into law in September that was named after Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator from South Carolina. The executive order suspends tariffs of up to 500% on US imports from Russia and 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil and natural gas. In other words, Congress built a new economic weapon to use against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has decided not to fire it — at least for now. “This eviscerates any real enforcement of the Lindsey Graham sanctions act,” said Ed Mills, Washington policy analyst at financial firm Raymond James. Mills noted that the move falls within a “pattern” for Trump, who similarly left Russia off the list of countries facing sweeping tariffs in April 2025. “The timing of the announcement is telling. Friday news dumps are done for the actions you don’t want noticed and politically you don’t want to defend,” Mills said. “This is certainly not the closing argument the GOP wanted weeks before the midterms.” The tariff pause helped ease intense pressure in the energy market — but only slightly. Oil futures dipped Monday morning as traders bet that fewer sanctions on Russia will mean more energy supply. And by early Monday afternoon, Brent crude, the world benchmark, flirted with five-month highs around $110 a barrel. “Russia is already selling crude oil to China, India, Turkey and elsewhere while they have been limiting exports of refined fuels,” said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. “The waiver may make it easier to sell oil to a wider range of customers, but whether it leads to additional supplies reaching the market is another question.” The executive order was met by praise from Kirill Dmitriev, head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, who hailed it on X as “an important and truly historic moment.” ‘Capitulating to a Russian dictator’ Multiple Republicans broke with Trump over the decision to scrap the Russia sanctions, including Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who is filling her late brother’s seat and running for a full term. “I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia to end the war and get the gas prices down because I don’t trust (Russian President Vladimir) Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” she said. Outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis blasted the move as “beyond irresponsible” and slammed Trump for “capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day.” Trump officials defended the decision to waive Russia sanctions. Over the weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the executive order gives Trump time to “study” the global economic impact of the sanctions. “The problem is that these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries — India, for example, and others,” Rubio said. “I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy.” Highest tariffs in nearly a century The decision was a surprise to some analysts, given Trump’s embrace of tariffs. Mills said many expected Trump might opt to only lightly enforce the Graham Act sanctions, but not to explicitly pause the tariffs altogether. Last year, Trump spiked US tariffs on imports to the highest level since the 1930s, according to John Iselin, associate director of economic analysis at The Budget Lab at Yale University. Although US tariffs have since eased — due to a series of pauses with China, a Supreme Court decision against Trump’s global tariffs and other developments — they are still higher than at any point between the 1940s and 2024.

articles.title: GM Q3 earnings preview: 'Core' franchise likely doing well with guidance in focus
articles.summary: GM (GM) will report third quarter results before the bell Tuesday, with investors expecting the Big Three automaker to keep growing profit, and perhaps up it...
articles.body:
GM ( GM ) will report third quarter results before the bell Tuesday, with investors expecting the Big Three automaker to keep growing profit and perhaps raise its guidance.

For the quarter, GM is expected to report Q3 revenue of $48.52 billion per Bloomberg consensus, slightly above last quarter's $48.03 billion. GM's adjusted earnings per share are estimated at $3.57, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.02 billion.

In addition to government offsets that are reducing its tariff bill, GM has spent the past year reworking its supply chain, shifting production, and negotiating with suppliers to blunt the tariff hit.

That allowed GM to raise its full-year 2026 guidance for a second time this year after the release of Q2 results.

Adjusted EBIT of 14.0billion-16.0 billion (prior 13.5billion-15.5 billion)

Adjusted EPS of 12.00-14.00 (prior 11.50-13.50)

Adjusted automotive free cash flow of 9.5billion-11.5 billion (prior 9billion-11 billion)

Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives believes GM will satisfy investors with its Q3 numbers.

"We believe the print will show the core franchise doing what it has done all year: producing the cash and pricing discipline that fund the software and autonomy roadmap at the center of our thesis," he wrote in a note to clients on Monday.

Ives has an Outperform rating on GM, with a $100 price target.

While profits have been growing, overall sales have been slipping.

Earlier this month, GM reported third quarter US sales of 670,974 vehicles , a drop of 5.5% compared to a year ago, as a collapse in EV sales offset gains from its pickups and small SUV s.

Based on GM's model-by-model figures, EV sales fell about 62% to roughly 25.5K units, shrinking to under 4% of GM's US volume from more than 9% a year ago. Excluding EVs, GM's sales were essentially flat, up 0.3%.

Sales of the Chevrolet Equinox EV plunged 92.4% to 1,905, the Blazer EV dropped 84.4%, the GMC Hummer EV slid 72.9%, and the Cadillac Lyriq fell 50.5%.

GM's gas-powered trucks helped deflect EV losses. Light-duty pickup sales rose 9.3%, led by a 13.3% jump in the Chevrolet Silverado light-duty to 100,221, while the GMC Sierra light-duty gained 2.9%. Heavy-duty models were softer, with the Silverado HD down 10.1% and the Sierra HD off 6.9%. GM said it is on track to lead the full-size pickup segment for a seventh straight year.

Despite decent financial performance for GM this year and boosted guidance, the stock is only marginally higher for the year, up around 1.6%.

Pras Subramanian is Lead Auto Reporter for Yahoo Finance. You can follow him on X and on Instagram .

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting device has Saudi backing: Prosecutor
articles.summary: US federal prosecutors allege the defendant was in frequent contact with unnamed member of royal family.
articles.body:
An ex-OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company appears to have received considerable support from the Saudi government, United States prosecutors have said in a court filing.

Federal prosecutors allege that the defendant, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was in frequent communication with an unnamed member of the Saudi royal family and that a Saudi military official paid for a one-way plane ticket for Alfozan’s wife and young son to return to Saudi Arabia after his arrest, according to the court document, made public late on Sunday.

Prosecutors made those allegations as they asked a federal judge to keep Alfozan in US custody to await trial, arguing he is a flight risk. Alfozan, a Saudi national and lawful permanent resident in the US, is scheduled to appear in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday.

The case has highlighted security challenges around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for an edge in the transformational technology.

“The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in — and making plans to travel to — Saudi Arabia,” prosecutors wrote in a detention memo.

The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A lawyer for Alfozan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawyer, William Pernik, previously asked for Alfozan to be released from custody, subject to conditions including location monitoring and surrendering his passport, and said Alfozan had spent the last 15 years in the US and had applied to become a citizen.

The lawyer said a planned trip by Alfozan to Saudi Arabia this month was booked before he was under investigation and was for “family and immigration reasons”, according to a court filing.

US prosecutors charged Alfozan last week with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan plugged a recording device into the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of OpenAI’s San Francisco buildings, according to a criminal complaint.

Meetings involving government officials took place in the conference room around the time the device was installed, according to the prosecutors’ detention memo.

Prosecutors said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be brought against Alfozan.

A member of the Saudi royal family sought to recruit Alfozan for an AI-focused role in Saudi Arabia, writing in one message, “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!” Alfozan replied, “100,” according to messages cited by prosecutors.

Before his arrest, Alfozan was scheduled to fly to Riyadh during a planned two-month parental leave. His wife told investigators that she and their son planned to move permanently to Saudi Arabia and that Alfozan eventually intended to join them, according to prosecutors.

In an Arabic-language interview on the Identity Capital podcast last month, Alfozan said that he visits Saudi Arabia three or four times a year, follows developments there and advises or mentors Saudi startups.

He said meeting Prince Mohammed bin Salman, then deputy crown prince, during a 2016 gathering with young Saudi tech workers in Silicon Valley persuaded him to learn at a top tech company before bringing those skills back home.

While Alfozan was working at Facebook, he and other Saudis in Silicon Valley formed a consulting initiative that linked Saudi public- and private-sector organisations with expertise in big data, the internet of things and machine learning.

OpenAI previously said it discovered the device on September 30 and referred the matter to the FBI.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the Saudi embassy for comment.

articles.title: Jon Stewart to stay at ‘The Daily Show’ through the 2028 election
articles.summary: Jon Stewart will remain at the helm of Comedy Central’s “The Daily Show” through December 2028, extending his once-a-week hosting role through the next presidential election.
articles.body: Jon Stewart will remain at the helm of Comedy Central’s “The Daily Show” through December 2028, extending his once-a-week hosting role through the next presidential election. Skydance announced the two-year extension on Monday, resolving uncertainty about Stewart’s contract, which was due to expire in December. The new deal means one of television’s most prominent critics of President Donald Trump is staying in place for the rest of Trump’s term. Stewart will continue hosting on Monday nights, an arrangement in place since January 2024, and serving as executive producer of the series. The satirical newscast’s correspondents “will continue to share hosting duties Tuesday – Thursday,” Skydance said. The agreement is Stewart’s longest extension since returning to the program, following two successive one-year renewals. And it is one of the first major programming announcements from the newly enlarged Skydance, which was formed earlier this month when Paramount Skydance acquired Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN’s parent company. “Jon Stewart is a generational talent and The Daily Show continues to be one of the most influential franchises on television and a cornerstone of Comedy Central,” George Cheeks, Skydance TV’s co-chair and chief content officer, said in a statement. “We are excited to continue our partnership with Jon and his award winning news team.” The decision to keep Stewart comes amid financial and political scrutiny of late-night television — including last year’s decision by Paramount’s prior management to cancel “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.” Stewart was an executive producer of his friend Colbert’s show and harshly criticized the cancellation, rejecting Paramount’s financial justification and accusing the company of bending the knee to the president. Viewers wondered at the time if Stewart might be next to be canceled, especially given Skydance chief David Ellison’s efforts to establish close ties with the Trump administration. Ellison hosted a dinner honoring the president earlier this year, and after the Warner merger closed, Trump praised Ellison and his father, billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, as “terrific people.” When Ellison was asked about Trump after the merger took effect, Ellison emphasized that his company had relationships with politicians from both parties in the US. “It’s important to talk to everyone on both sides of the aisle,” he said. “We don’t want to politicize.” Stewart originally left “The Daily Show” in 2015, handing the program to Trevor Noah, who departed in December 2022. Stewart’s 2024 return brought a familiar face back to the franchise during that presidential election cycle, and this new agreement keeps him in place through the next one.

articles.title: The richest members of Congress in 2026
articles.summary: Congress’ wealthiest members, according to the most recently published live net worth estimates tracked by Quiver Quantitative.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Several of Congress’ wealthiest lawmakers are preparing to leave office after this term. Others are on the ballot as the midterms approach .

Members of the House and Senate must file annual financial disclosures under the Ethics in Government Act . The report lists their investments, assets and business interests.

Here are Congress’ wealthiest members, according to the most recently published live net worth estimates tracked by Quiver Quantitative .

Rep. Jefferson Shreve (R-Ind.) sits at the top of Quiver’s list with an estimated net worth of $715.2 million. He’s a former Indianapolis city council member.

His fortune comes from the self-storage business Storage Express, which he sold for $590 million in 2022.

Shreve narrowly survived a primary challenge in May and will face Democratic nominee Cynthia “Cinde” Wirth in November, a rematch of 2024.

Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) is Congress’ second-richest member on Quiver’s list, with a net worth of $664.4 million, though he has many debts.

Forbes once estimated Justice’s fortune at $1.9 billion, stripped him of his billionaire status in 2021, and in 2025, estimated his net worth fell below zero because his liabilities far exceeded his assets.

He also agreed to pay nearly $5.2 million in overdue personal taxes after the IRS filed liens of more than $8 million against him and his wife.

Justice won his seat in 2024. His term runs through 2030.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) led most wealth lists last year, though Quiver now estimates he is worth $509.4 million, the third highest in Congress.

Before entering politics, Scott co-founded HCA Healthcare and Solantic. He served as Florida’s governor from 2011 to 2019.

Scott’s next race is the 2030 Florida Senate election.

Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) made his fortune as CEO of car-alarm maker Directed Electronics. Quiver estimates his worth at $399.3 million as of May 24, the fourth highest in Congress.

Issa ended his reelection campaign on March 6 and endorsed San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond as his replacement. California’s new congressional map turned his district from solidly Republican into one that slightly favors Democrats.

Rep. Vern Buchanan (R-Fla.) built his wealth through car dealerships, an aircraft leasing company and Speedy Printing. Quiver estimated his net worth at $272.1 million.

Buchanan announced Jan. 27 that he would not seek reelection .

Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) is the richest Democrat in Congress on Quiver’s list, with an estimated net worth of $262.4 million. Most of that wealth comes from her husband Paul Pelosi’s stock holdings .

Pelosi was the first woman to serve as House Speaker and has been in Congress since 1987. She announced last year she would not run again after her current term ends in 2027 and endorsed San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan in the race to succeed her.

Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) made his money in telecommunications venture capital, including an early role in what became Nextel. His net worth is estimated at $210.1 million.

Warner is seeking a fourth term against Republican Bert Mizusawa. He has said this will be his last reelection campaign.

Rep. Daniel Goldman (D-N.Y.) is an heir to the Levi Strauss fortune. His net worth is estimated at $208 million.

Former New York city comptroller Brad Lander defeated Goldman in the June 23 Democratic primary, roughly 66 percent to 34 percent.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is the eldest son of TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts. Quiver estimates his net worth at $206.6 million. He was Nebraska’s governor from 2015 to 2023.

Ricketts is on the ballot in one of the country’s most closely watched Senate races. His opponent is independent Dan Osborn , a union mechanic who has focused on Ricketts’ family wealth in the race.

Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-Md.) is a first-term lawmaker with a net worth estimated at $199.1 million. She is a lawyer and former Commerce Department official. Her husband, former Rep. John Delaney, held the same seat from 2013 to 2019.

Delaney beat former Rep. David Trone in the June primary, 48 percent to 36 percent, and now faces Republican Robin Ficker in November.

articles.title: Hassett dismisses negative economic polls: ‘We are in a boom’
articles.summary: Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), dismissed recent polling Monday, instead arguing the U.S. economy is “in a boom.” During an interview on CNBC’s “Squawk Box,” Hassett said consumer spending indicates the economy remains strong. “If economic polls … were correct, then people wouldn’t be taking trips to nice hotels, they…
articles.body:
Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), dismissed recent polling Monday, instead arguing the U.S. economy is “in a boom.”

During an interview on CNBC’s “Squawk Box,” Hassett said consumer spending indicates the economy remains strong.

“If economic polls … were correct, then people wouldn’t be taking trips to nice hotels, they wouldn’t be flying, they wouldn’t be buying cars, they wouldn’t be doing all the things they do when they’re feeling good about the economy,” the NEC director told host Joe Kernen.

Consumer spending increased by $190.7 billion from July to August, a figure that took into account the annual inflation rate of 3.4 percent , as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.

Hassett argued Monday that “true sentiment” of the economy is “best measured by what you see” Americans doing.

“And what people are doing is they’re acting like we’re in a boom. And the reason they’re doing that is because despite what the polls say, we are in a boom,” he told Kernen.

Consumer confidence declined in September to its lowest level since 2014, according to the Conference Board .

The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers index has also preliminarily reported that consumer confidence was at a reading of 46.3 in October, down 13.6 percent year-over-year. The survey will release final data for this month Friday.

While the unemployment rate remains below 5 percent , inflation is still running above the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target rate. Annual inflation in September was 3.7 percent , up from 3.4 percent in August , according to the consumer price index .

Persistent inflation compelled Federal Reserve officials to raise interest rates last month for the first time since the summer of 2023. Traders are pricing in a roughly 83 percent chance of the central bank holding rates steady at its meeting next week , according to the CME FedWatch tool .

The average 30-year mortgage rate, at 7.4 percent, is also at a nearly four-year high, according to Freddie Mac .

But Hassett, echoing President Trump’s positive view of the economy, said Monday that the country is in good shape as early voting in the midterms is underway.

“If you look at, holistically, where the economy is, we’ve got high growth, we’ve got the lowest unemployment insurance claims since World War II,” Hassett told Kernen, arguing September’s uptick in inflation is “hardly enough to overpower all the good news” for the economy.

articles.title: Trade margins on 137 cancer drugs capped, but will bills get lower?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Govt’s move to cap trade margins at 30% of MRP on 137 cancer drugs, covering over 1,000 medicine brands, puts the focus on actual patient
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Govt’s move to cap trade margins at 30% of MRP on 137 cancer drugs, covering over 1,000 medicine brands, puts the focus on actual patient savings, with effective implementation and monitoring needed to ensure it translates into lower medical bills.The cap could narrow the gap between prices at which medicines are supplied to hospitals and their MRPs, but it may have a limited impact on overall cost of healthcare as hospitals may seek to offset lower margins by raising charges on consumables, diagnostics or procedures, public health and industry experts told TOI. A similar trend was seen after cardiac stent prices were capped in 2017, when several private hospital chains raised angioplasty package rates, they said.Wider rationalisation of margins across products needed: ExpertsExperts said wider rationalisation of margins across medical products, alongside closer scrutiny of hospital charges, may be needed to substantially reduce medical bills. Hospital stocks were down on BSE on Monday, following the govt notification on Oct 17.The MRP of certain cancer drugs are up to Rs 5 lakh per vial or pack, including a combination of pertuzumab and trastuzumab, atezolizumab, teclistamab, inotuzumab ozogamicin and daratumumab.“The success of this measure will, however, depend equally on timely implementation across manufacturers, distributors and hospitals. A trade margin of 30% should not be misconstrued as a 30% profit margin for hospitals. The defined trade margin applies across the distribution chain, and the basis of calculation and applicability of the prescribed margin at different stages of the supply chain, should be clearly communicated to avoid any misunderstanding,” Girdhar Gyani, director general at the Association of Healthcare Providers, which represents over 20,000 hospitals and healthcare providers, told TOI.Oncology is a significant revenue stream for hospitals, with expensive cancer drugs and cost of care contributing to high treatment costs. The margin cap could put pressure on hospital earnings, raising concerns over whether lower margins could affect the viability of such services. “Affordability must be viewed across the entire cancer-care pathway, from screening and diagnosis to treatment,” said Mayur Sirdesai, co-founding partner at Somerset Indus Capital.“The impact of TMR on affordability and patient access will need to be evaluated, said Sudarshan Jain, secretary-general of Indian Pharmaceutical Alliance.Public health experts said the margin rationalisation may not be enough to reduce costs for patients. “Prices of these medicines will still remain out of the reach for many patients. articles.title: The 10-year Treasury yield is above 5%. Should savers lock in now?
articles.summary: Treasury yields have climbed above 5%. Here's whether locking in a higher yield makes sense for your savings.
articles.body:

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield closed at 5.09% on Friday, according to the Treasury's daily par yield curve. Yields have retreated from recent highs but remain above 5% as concerns about persistent inflation and potentially higher interest rates continue to put pressure on markets.

For savers, higher yields could present a unique opportunity to lock in a fixed rate for a longer term, especially as they look for ways to keep pace with rising inflation.

However, whether a 10-year Treasury note is a worthwhile investment highly depends on your savings goals, when you'll need access to your money, and your tolerance for the risk of selling if rates change.

"If you are waiting on the Fed to push rates higher before you lock anything in, I would ask what exactly you are waiting for," said David Kassir, managing director of Private Wealth Management, Manna Wealth Management. "Nobody rings a bell at the top, and the income you collect while you wait is real money."

Why Treasurys can be appealing when rates are volatile

The Treasury yield is the return an investor receives for lending money to the government by buying a Treasury note . Interest is fixed and paid every six months until the end of your term, when you get your principal back.

Say you invest $1,000 in a 10-year Treasury note yielding approximately 5.1%. Your investment would generate an annualized return of about $51, assuming you hold the note to maturity. The actual cash interest payments depend on the note's coupon rate and purchase price.

If rates rise, your Treasury note becomes less valuable because investors can earn a higher rate on newly issued Treasurys. If rates fall, your Treasury note becomes more valuable, and you could sell your note before maturity and still recoup more than you originally invested.

You can sell a 10-year Treasury note before maturity through a bank, broker, or dealer. If you buy through TreasuryDirect, you must hold the note for at least 45 days before transferring it for sale. It's also important to remember that market prices and yields vary daily, so there's a chance you could sell at a loss if you sell before maturity.

The appeal of these notes is that they are backed by the U.S. government and pay a fixed rate, which can be reassuring when rates across other products keep fluctuating. The trade-off is that you're committing to a long-term investment in exchange for that fixed rate, and selling early could result in a loss.

Unlike other savings vehicles, such as high-yield savings accounts and money market accounts , you can count on a fixed rate that won't fluctuate with the current environment.

However, locking into a longer-term Treasury could mean missing out on potential savings if rates rise.

How Treasury notes compare to rates offered by other savings vehicles

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. To preserve your purchasing power, you'd need to earn 3.7% APY on your savings. However, to build long-term wealth, you'd want to opt for an account that earns even more.

A 10-year Treasury can certainly be a worthwhile investment to consider, but it's not your only option. Some experts suggest that pairing it with other types of savings vehicles for a more diversified approach can make the most sense. Especially because it's impossible to predict with complete certainty how returns across other products and investments will change over time.

A high-yield savings account or money market account could be a better option for savers who value more flexibility and greater access to their cash, while a shorter-term CD can be a middle ground for savers who want the benefit of a fixed rate, but may not be willing to commit to a 10-year term or are fearful that locking into a Treasury note now could lock them out of higher returns if rates continue to increase.

How to invest and decide whether now is the right time

You can buy Treasury securities through the TreasuryDirect website, or through a bank or broker. The investment minimum through TreasuryDirect is $100 and can be increased in increments of $100. Brokers may have minimums that start at $1,000.

Whether a long-term Treasury is right for you depends on your timeline for needing the money back, how much access you need to that money, and your savings goals.

Keeping tabs on how interest rates are changing can be valuable; however, experts caution savers against waiting for the "perfect" time to invest.

"For money you know you will need in the next year or two, I would not reach for duration just because the 10-year touched 5.10%," Kassir said. "But for longer-term money, especially retirees building an income ladder, these are the best yields we have seen in years, and I would rather ladder into them than sit in cash waiting for a perfect entry point nobody can time."

Bond yields rise as bond prices fall, impacting everything from stock and bond markets to loan rates and savings returns.
